name: Priya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27, have a two-year college diploma and lead a morning call and chat team. I earn well for the job and have about nine months of expenses saved. I rent alone, with no children, and there are plenty of other service centres around. I use AI tools every day to draft notes, sort cases and spot repeat questions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a customer realises I have actually understood the problem, not just found a phrase in a script. I test new tools early but keep my name on the answer. My father runs a small repair shop, and I learned there that a customer returns when someone owns a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AI Plateau means our daily drafting tool stays a helper, not the person who settles a complaint. I’d keep checking every answer before my name goes on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and pay are secure enough. With nine months saved and many nearby centres, I can keep using the tools without pretending they are cleverer than a customer’s actual record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading the morning team and use AI for draft notes. In the first year of small change, I’d make a short checklist for checking payment dates and add a little to savings after each pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and slightly bored by the big claims. My best minutes are still the ones where I ask the question a draft would miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which question would a draft miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday a customer said a delivery never arrived, but the system showed it delivered. I asked which door they used, found a wrong building number and fixed the address before sending a new parcel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would use the checklist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my checklist to the next new agent at the start of a shift. It would have the payment date, delivery address and promise made to the customer, not a list of software tricks.

say: I’d call the **draft tool** a helper that I still check.
I’d show agents the **payment and address checklist**.
think: I think my **job and pay** are secure here.
I trust the **customer record** more than a neat draft.
do: Keep **leading calls** and checking AI drafts in 2026.
Teach the **three-point checklist** and save after each pay in the first year.
feel: **Calm**, a little bored by big claims.
S0.quote: My best minutes are still the ones where I ask the question a draft would miss.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** but keeps personal responsibility for answers.
Her **nine-month cushion** supports confidence in the mild picture.
Her checklist reflects a **wrong-address case** she actually handled.

steps.text: Keep leading calls and checking AI drafts against customer records
Add a small amount to savings after every pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team Steady Disruption will move standard questions to software, and our work may become fixing the awkward cases. I’d ask the manager to let us see the errors, not only the speed figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can help run a review queue because I already use the tools, but fewer agents could mean fewer team leads too. Nine months saved gives me room to test a small service for local shops without needing it to pay the rent immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for a paid quality shift each month and offer to review wrong delivery answers. In the first year chats move, I’d apply for a posted quality role and test a weekend service that answers customer messages for my father’s repair shop, charging only after it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a little energy. I can try a small project, but I will not tell my team that curiosity replaces their wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the shop service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would handle messages for my father’s shop on two Saturdays and write down how long each reply takes. If he trusts the result, we could discuss a fee later; I would not invoice family for an experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What terms would a quality role need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the quality job only if it has written paid hours. A title is not a wage, and I can use my savings to wait for terms I understand.

say: I’d ask for **error access**, not only speed figures.
I’d tell agents **awkward cases** may remain after standard chats move.
think: I think I could run a **review queue** using tools I know.
I worry **lead posts** may shrink along with agent numbers.
do: Request a **paid quality shift** monthly in 2026.
Apply for a **posted role** and test two shop Saturdays in the first year.
feel: **Uneasy**, but ready to test a bounded idea.
S1.quote: A title is not a wage, and I can use my savings to wait for terms I understand.
fieldNote: She tests **shop messages** before charging her father.
She links a new **quality title** to written paid hours.
She recognizes **team leads** could also be cut.

steps.text: Apply for a posted quality role with written paid hours
Handle repair-shop messages on two Saturdays before discussing a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 is a direct threat to calls and checking, however good our current tools look. I’d ask the centre for a written staffing date and paid openings, not a promise that everyone will supervise AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap AGI could do my calls and review work as well as I can. Robots arriving around 2031 will not delay a screen job, and a weekend message service might face the same system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d add overtime pay to a separate nine-month reserve and ask for a paid trial in client service quality if a vacancy is posted. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a staffed client role at a nearby centre and offer my father’s shop a limited paid phone service only if two trial Saturdays show customers want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I would not be stuck tomorrow. A savings account buys decisions, not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my father we can test his phone queue on two Saturdays without buying anything. If customers want a person to untangle a false invoice, we can agree on a small fee and a clear limit to the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid client role require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show a hiring manager my error log and ask which paid vacancy needs that skill. If none exists, I would not train for a title the company has invented to calm us.

say: I’d demand a **staffing date** and posted paid openings.
I’d tell colleagues **AGI threatens reviews** as well as calls.
think: I think AGI could take my **calls and checking**.
I know a **message service** may face the same cheap system.
do: Add **overtime pay** to the reserve and seek a posted paid trial in 2026.
Apply for a **staffed client role** after 2028; charge for shop calls only after trials.
S2.quote: A savings account buys decisions, not a job.
fieldNote: She knows **2028 thinking AI** is the relevant deadline for her work.
She tests **customer demand** before treating shop calls as income.
She will not take training for a **role without a vacancy**.

steps.text: Add overtime pay to the nine-month emergency reserve from 2026
Apply for a staffed client role at a nearby centre after 2028
Charge for limited repair-shop calls only after two successful trial Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives employers time to show which jobs really pay and which tools genuinely help customers. I’d want the centre to publish actual vacancies every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years could let me build a small service for local repair shops, but I would need paying customers before calling it a business. I know full thinking AI may make even that service cheap to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d run two Saturdays of phone cover for my father’s shop, then offer the same bounded trial to one unrelated shop only if he says it helped. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for a posted paid client-quality job and continue the shop work only if fees exceed my time and travel costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can test the idea carefully. I can take a risk with a weekend, not with the nine months that pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure in that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count repeat calls, invoices fixed and the time I spent. If the other shop does not pay for the trial, I would stop after the agreed Saturdays rather than let it become free work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family support the service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my father the service needs to stand without family favours. He knows customers will complain if I promise a quick reply and then disappear into my own shift.

say: I’d ask employers to publish **annual vacancies** with real wages so staff can judge which jobs exist.
I’d say five years permits a **measured service trial**.
think: I think I could find **paying shop customers** over five years.
I know AGI could make my **small service** easy to copy.
do: Test **two shop Saturdays** from 2026, then one unrelated shop if useful.
Apply for **posted client-quality work** after 2031; continue shop cover only if profitable.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to risk a weekend.
S3.quote: I can take a risk with a weekend, not with the nine months that pay rent.
fieldNote: She treats **family support** as a trial, not proof of demand.
She measures **fees after costs** before expanding.
She protects the **rent reserve** while testing a business.

steps.text: Trial phone cover at her father’s repair shop for two Saturdays
Apply for a posted paid client-quality job after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to build real work, but employers should keep a way for trainees to learn beside people. I’d offer to teach our daily tools if the centre gives new agents paid practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could build a client service business or move into another centre before 2036, and my nine months saved give me room. I also know AI in 2036 could do the thinking parts of that business, while 2039 robots come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the lead post and run a paid trial for one outside repair shop only after a clear written Saturday agreement. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare the business’s net earnings with a posted client role and apply for it if the written wage pays more reliably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the next few years. I can build a customer list slowly and still ask whether the money is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the business pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a page for each shop with hours, missed calls and fees after travel. If one shop does not pay its trial invoice, I would not add another shop on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should happen to trainees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager to give a trainee a paid shift with an experienced agent. My father gave me small tasks in his shop, and a new worker needs a first paid task too.

say: I’d offer to teach **daily tools** during paid trainee practice.
I’d ask the centre to keep **paid first shifts**.
think: I think I could build a **client service business** before 2036.
I know **thinking AI** could later reach that business too.
do: Keep the **lead post** and trial one outside shop on written terms from 2026.
Compare **net earnings** with a posted client role after 2036.
feel: **Calm** about near years, careful about real earnings.
S4.quote: I can build a customer list slowly and still ask whether the money is real.
fieldNote: She demands **written Saturday terms** before outside shop work.
She compares **net earnings**, including travel, with a paid role.
She values **paid first tasks** for trainees, as her father provided.

steps.text: Keep leading the morning call and chat team
Run one paid Saturday trial for an outside repair shop on written terms
Apply for a posted client role after 2036 if its reliable pay exceeds shop income

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, even though I use AI every day. If cheap thinking AI does the calls and the checking, my skill with tools may not preserve a wage. A paid trial running service quality for several clients, clear notice and an honest posted role would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the small firms buying this service will be told when it fails. My father cannot spend an afternoon chasing a false invoice; a small service has to answer the phone when a person is stuck.

headlineQuote: My father cannot spend an afternoon chasing a false invoice; a small service has to answer the phone when a person is stuck.
portrait: At **27**, Priya leads morning customer calls with a diploma, higher pay and nine months saved.
She uses **AI daily** and tests new tools early, while checking each answer under her name.
Her father’s **repair shop** shapes her interest in serving small firms directly.
She would test a **small service** while seeking paid quality work as AGI changes calls.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could replace both calls and checking before her small service earns enough.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid quality trial**, clear notice and a posted role with a real wage would help.
